faq.q: Can I use these examples to plan a video for my product?
faq.a: Yes. Upload a sharp product photo, choose the format and length available in the workspace, then describe one clear opening scene. Try another version when you want a different opening.

faq.q: Why don't the examples include prices or headlines?
faq.a: AI sometimes garbles letters and numbers, so prices, headlines and offers are left for you to add in Canva, CapCut or Ads Manager, where every word and number stays exactly as you type it.

faq.q: What can I learn from the product video examples?
faq.a: Use the examples to compare openings, camera movement, and product framing. Build your own version with a sharp photo, a chosen size, and one clear action.

faq.q: How do I choose between a photo and video example?
faq.a: Use photo examples to plan listing, lifestyle, or detail images. Use video examples when movement or a product action helps explain how the item is used.

overview.h2: How to read a product example
overview.p: Each card shows an example product photo, scene direction, and generated result. Look first at the product's outline, color, closure, label area, and other buying details; then look at the new setting or camera movement. The useful question is whether the result gives shoppers a new reason to understand that product.

overview.h2: Use the gallery as a starting point
overview.p: These examples show possible directions for your own product. They are prompts for a scene, not a promise that every result will include every prop, hand, reflection, or fold from your photo. Start with the closest product type, borrow its level of detail, and make a separate version when you want another opening or setting.

input_guide.h2: Prepare a source photo that can be compared

items.d: Keep the product in focus, uncropped, and large enough to inspect. For shoes, bags, jewelry, or electronics, photograph every side you expect the gallery to show.

items.t: Keep one product in the frame
items.d: A single item makes it easier to tell whether the shape and color stayed consistent. If two products are the point of the comparison, make that relationship explicit in the description.

items.t: Describe one scene at a time
items.d: Name the place, light, action, and useful framing detail: for example, a coffee bag beside a pour-over brewer on a bright kitchen counter. Save a second action for a new version.
Do not rely on generated lettering for a price, date, headline, or discount code. Keep open space where your message can go, then type the final words after download.

results.h2: What each result can help you decide

items.d: A packshot, close-up, side view, or size cue helps a shopper judge the object before ordering. Use it beside the main image when the shape or materials need more explanation.
A lifestyle scene shows where an item belongs: on a vanity, desk, breakfast table, street, or bath ledge. Choose a setting that makes sense for how the product is used.
A square image can give a scrolling feed a clear product moment and room for your own offer. Add the message in the ad tool so every number stays accurate.
Change one meaningful variable, such as the opening scene or background, and make another job. Keeping the product and the rest of the direction steady gives you a cleaner comparison.
Phone case on a tidy desk beside earbuds and a notebook; a hand picks it up and turns the camera cutout toward the light.
Silver necklace on a dark top at a neckline; move from the worn view to a close view of the pendant so shoppers can judge length and size.
Kraft coffee bag on a kitchen counter beside a pour-over brewer, then at a breakfast table with a mug and croissant.
Teal yoga mat rolled with its strap in a bright room, then unrolled while someone stretches beside a window.
Red hot-sauce bottle on a rustic table with fresh chilies; a pour over tacos gives the clip one clear action.
White candle jar on a living-room coffee table with books and a knit throw, then on a bath ledge beside a folded towel.

after_download.h2: Finish the example before you publish

items.d: Put the downloaded result beside the item you ship. Check color, proportions, logos, labels, buttons, edges, and the number of pieces before a shopper sees it.
Place the price, date, offer, headline, captions, and music in Canva, CapCut, TikTok, Ads Manager, or your usual editor. Type the details yourself to keep campaign wording accurate.
AI-generated people are not customers. Keep the text focused on the product and check the current disclosure guidance for the platform where you post the image or clip.

good: Sellers building a listing gallery from one clear product photo
Small shops that need a few distinct settings for social posts or feed ads
Marketers comparing openings, scenes, or formats for the same product
Products whose use, scale, or setting is easier to understand in a picture or short clip
not_ideal: Exact small lettering, prices, dates, or technical specifications that must be copied without errors
A customer testimonial or review, because generated people are not real buyers
A hidden side or unseen feature; provide a source photo for every view you need to show
